title: What does 5.5 overs left really mean?
description: A scoreboard shows overs left as five point five. Since an over has six balls, the five after the point counts balls and not tenths. Other places where a point is not a decimal are named. Keeko's doubt reads it as five and a half overs.
teaching_notes: One idea: a point does not always mean a decimal, so first ask what the digits count. Watch for students who read overs and balls as a decimal of tenths.

source: A scoreboard shows 'Overs left: 5.5'. How many overs and ba
video_script.why: The child reads a point in a decimal as tenths, and now sees places where the point only separates two different counts.
video_script.substitution: Ask what the digits count, then read the part after the point in the unit it counts, here balls in an over.
video_script.anchor: A cricket scoreboard that shows overs left as 5.5.
video_script.wrong_move: Reads 5.5 overs as a decimal, five and a half overs, and takes half of six balls as three balls.
video_script.payoff_line: A point is not always a decimal point

final_answer.value: 5 5/6 overs, that is 5 overs and 5 balls
final_answer.spoken: five and five sixths overs, that is five overs and five balls

hold_back: 5 5/6 overs, that is 5 overs and 5 balls
maths_rules: 1 over = 6 balls, so 1 ball = 1/6 of an over
5 balls = 5/6 of an over, so 5.5 overs = 5 5/6 overs
the slip: 0.5 as a decimal is half, and half of 6 balls is 3 balls, which is not 5 balls
2.30 is 2 hours 30 minutes, 5.11 is 5 feet 11 inches, 2.10 is the second of October, 1.10 is a version of an app
video_script.design: A row of six balls makes one over. The five after the point lights five of the six balls, so it is read as five sixths and not as five tenths. Four small cards then show other places where a point only separates two counts.
